extracted.intended_audience: scientifically literate general readers, scientists, and philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative principles for scientific inquiry and belief-formation — i.e., what counts as good reasoning, how to initiate and end inquiry, and comparisons of methods for fixing belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of reasoning (true conclusion from true premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The object of reasoning is to find out, from the consideration of what we already know, something else which we do not know. Consequently, reasoning is good if it be such as to give a true conclusion from true premises, and not otherwise."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity is a factual relation: given premises A and conclusion B, the question is whether those facts are so related that if A is, B is. It is not a psychological question of whether we feel an impulse to accept the conclusion. A valid inference must produce a true conclusion from true premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the guiding principle or habit of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: "The habit is good or otherwise, according as it produces true conclusions from true premises... The particular habit of mind which governs this or that inference may be formulated in a proposition whose truth depends on the validity of the inferences which the habit determines; and such a formula is called a guiding principle of inference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a guiding principle reliably produces true conclusions in general. Example: inferring that what is true of one piece of copper is true of another — this guiding principle is safer for copper than for brass. Select guiding principles appropriate to the similarity class involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement of opinion as the sole object of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hence, the sole object of inquiry is the settlement of opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiry is motivated by doubt and terminates when belief (settlement of opinion) is reached. Although we may fancy we seek 'true' opinion, practically the aim of inquiry is to obtain a belief that one thinks to be true; once a firm belief is attained, mental effort on the subject ceases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine doubt as necessary motive for inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: "There must be a real and living doubt, and without this all discussion is idle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely phrasing a question (putting a proposition in interrogative form) is insufficient to start real inquiry. Actual psychological irritation of doubt is required to stimulate the struggle to attain belief (inquiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premises need not be absolutely indubitable to demonstrate
rubrics_metrics.description: "An inquiry, to have that completely satisfactory result called demonstration, has only to start with propositions perfectly free from all actual doubt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand philosophical absolute certainty as a prerequisite; start from premises that are free from actual, practical doubt. If premises are not doubted in fact, they are as satisfactory as possible for demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of tenacity (fixing belief by willful maintenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This method of fixing belief, which may be called the method of tenacity, will be unable to hold its ground in practice... [people] cling spasmodically to the views they already take."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by excluding contrary information and constant reiteration of a chosen answer. Pros: yields peace of mind for the individual and can be psychologically effective. Cons: socially unstable (others disagree), vulnerable to social influence, and fail as a general method for community knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of authority (institutional fixation of belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let the will of the state act... an institution... to keep correct doctrines before the attention of the people, to reiterate them perpetually... to prevent contrary doctrines from being taught..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful for large-scale, persistent fixation of beliefs (cultural stability, monumental accomplishments), and superior to tenacity for social cohesion; but it often involves suppression, cruelty, slow change, and cannot attend to every subject. Its 'success' is judged internally by the authority, not by independent truth-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori (development/taste) method of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: The a priori method (development by what is 'agreeable to reason' or by taste) leads to adoption of systems because fundamental propositions seem agreeable to reason rather than because of observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectually respectable in appearance, but liable to fashion, accidental causes, and disagreement; metaphysical development tends to swing between extremes and lacks convergence to truth. It does not eliminate dependence on accidental human causes and so fails as a general method for fixing true opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of science / true induction (external permanency and reproducibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The method of science... Its fundamental hypothesis... There are real things, whose characters are entirely independent of our opinions about them; those realities affect our senses according to regular laws... by taking advantage of the laws of perception, we can ascertain by reasoning how things really are, and any man, if he have sufficient experience and reason enough about it, will be led to the one true conclusion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science fixes belief by appeal to realities independent of individual/human preference, employing reproducible experience, verification, and reason. It is the only method that admits a distinction of right and wrong application; experience and scientific investigation provide convergent, public, corrective tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and wrong application of methods (normativity within science)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is the only one of the four methods which presents any distinction of a right and a wrong way... the only test on [other methods] is what the [authorities or tendencies] think... The very essence of [scientific] method is that it can be pursued wrongly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific method has objective standards (proper experimental design, correct use of induction, verification); other methods lack internal criteria for right/wrong. Evaluate not just method choice but correct execution according to scientific norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of generalization across similar cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Example given: observing a rotating copper disk comes to rest between magnet poles and inferring this will happen with every disk of copper — guiding principle: what is true of one piece of copper is true of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the scope of generalization (class membership, relevant similarities). Some guiding principles are safer for certain substances (copper) than for others (brass); explicit attention to class and relevant differences is necessary before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical action-guiding reliability of beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our beliefs guide our desires and shape our actions... The feeling of believing is... an indication of there being established in our nature some habit which will determine our actions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normative test of a belief is whether it reliably guides action in accordance with desired outcomes. Because belief has behavioral consequences, inquiry should favor beliefs that will successfully guide actions when the occasion arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-setting and transparency of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The subject could hardly be treated, however, without being first limited... there exists a division among facts... between those which are necessarily taken for granted in asking whether a certain conclusion follows from certain premises, and those which are not implied in that question."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before tackling reasoning problems, clearly delimit the inquiry and state which facts/assumptions are taken for granted. Distinguish essential background assumptions from items of research interest to avoid confusion and improper inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding metaphysical confusion between logical/conceptual products and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: "A quality as such is never an object of observation. We can see that a thing is blue or green, but the quality of being blue... are not things which we see; they are products of logical reflection... common-sense... is deeply imbued with that bad logical quality to which the epithet metaphysical is commonly applied; and nothing can clear it up but a severe course of logic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of treating abstract logical/conceptual entities as directly observed facts. Maintain clarity between observable phenomena and concepts derived by reflection; rigorous logical analysis helps prevent conflation and confusion in inquiry.
